name: Self-Driving Laboratories
title: Self-Driving Laboratories
answer: Self-driving laboratories are lab systems that close the loop between experiment design, execution, measurement, and analysis, so that software and hardware can propose and run the next experiment with limited human intervention. They sit at the intersection of laboratory automation, simulation, and machine learning, and they are studied as a way to speed up discovery in chemistry, materials, biology, and related fields. The scope includes the orchestration software, the robotic platforms, the sensors and instruments, and the models that decide what to try next. It also includes the simulation environments used to pre-test campaigns before they touch physical samples. The site's library holds 135 research papers and 11795 claims extracted from research works, which shows the depth of the surrounding literature.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A self-driving lab runs on a stack that starts with physical automation, such as liquid handlers, robotic arms, plate readers, pumps, and environmental controls, all connected through scheduling and control software. Sensors and analytical instruments feed measurements back into a data layer, which may include databases, file stores, and message queues. Compute for model training and experiment planning can sit on local servers or in the cloud, depending on latency, data volume, and site policy. Simulation engines and digital twins provide a safe place to test candidate experiments before they are run on real materials. The site's catalogue lists 800 scientific models and 732 AI tools, which reflects the range of components that can appear in such a stack.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done as a loop: a model or planner proposes a batch of experiments, the scheduler dispatches them to instruments, the instruments produce measurements, and the results update the model for the next round. Common methods include Bayesian optimization, active learning, design of experiments, and surrogate models that approximate expensive simulations. Human researchers set objectives, constraints, and safety bounds, then review results and adjust the campaign. Simulation can be used to warm-start the loop or to explore regions that are impractical to test physically. Provenance is kept by logging parameters, instrument settings, raw data, and model versions so that a run can be reconstructed.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance in self-driving labs cover data ownership, attribution, safety, and reproducibility. Because experiments are generated and executed automatically, audit trails matter: who set the objective, which model version proposed the experiment, what instrument settings were used, and where the raw data landed. Intellectual property and licensing questions can arise when a lab uses third-party models, robotic platforms, or simulation software, and when results are published. Safety governance includes chemical, biological, and physical hazards, with limits encoded in the planner and enforced by the scheduler. The site links to original papers rather than to the Consensus search tool, which supports provenance by pointing readers to the primary source.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward tighter integration between simulation and physical experiments, so that campaigns can transfer policies learned in silico to real instruments. Standards for experiment description, data schemas, and model interfaces are likely to matter more as labs mix hardware and software from different sources. Foundation models and other large pretrained systems are being explored for experiment planning, though their role in closed-loop control remains an active area. Benchmarks and shared tasks will help compare self-driving lab approaches across domains. The site's 686 glossary terms and 91 AI books suggest that the vocabulary and background material around the topic are still expanding.
